{{Short description|Study of Hopf algebras via their actions on vector spaces and associative algebras}}

In [[abstract algebra]], a '''representation of a [[Hopf algebra]]''' is a [[algebra representation|representation]] of its underlying [[associative algebra]].<ref name="i427">{{cite web | title=Introduction to Hopf algebras and representations | url=https://math.aalto.fi/~kkytola/files_KK/lectures_files_KK/Hopf-lecture_notes.pdf |publisher=AALTO| access-date=2025-12-02}}</ref><ref name="i015">{{cite book | last1=Roggenkamp | first1=Klaus W. | last2=Stefanescu | first2=Mirela | title=Algebra - Representation Theory | publisher=Springer Science & Business Media | date=2001-08-31 | isbn=978-0-7923-7113-7 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=dtsUcQTHPqYC&q=Representation+theory+of+Hopf+algebras | access-date=2025-12-02}}</ref> 
The [[representation theory]] of Hopf algebras is of particular interest because it has more structure than that of more general associative algebras; in particular, there exist [[Dual representation|duals]] and [[Tensor product of representations|tensor products]], similarly to the representations of [[finite groups]] and [[Lie algebras]].

These natural operations on the [[Category (mathematics)|category]] of representations of a Hopf algebra (whose objects are the representations and whose morphism are the [[Representation theory#Equivariant maps and isomorphisms|equivariant maps]]) give it additional structure:
* The existence of tensor products (and trivial representations) make the category of representations into a [[monoidal category]],<ref name=grabowski2025>{{Cite book |last=Grabowski |first=Jan E. |title=Representation Theory: A Categorical Approach |date=2025-09-22 |publisher=Open Book Publishers |isbn=978-1-80511-714-8 |edition=1 |location=Cambridge, UK |language=en |doi=10.11647/OBP.0492| pages=202–206 |doi-access=free }}</ref>
* The existence of duals makes this category [[rigid monoidal category|rigid]],<ref name=grabowski2025/>
* If <math>H</math> is [[Quasitriangular Hopf algebra|quasitiangular]], the category is [[Braided monoidal category|braided monoidal]],<ref name=montgomery1993>{{citation | last=Montgomery | first=Susan | author-link=Susan Montgomery|title=Hopf algebras and their actions on rings | series=Regional Conference Series in Mathematics | volume=82 | location=Providence, Rhode Island | publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]] | year=1993 | isbn=978-0-8218-0738-5 | zbl=0793.16029 }}</ref>
* If <math>H</math> is [[Coalgebra#Further concepts and facts|co-commutative]], or more generally if it is triangular, the category is [[Symmetric monoidal category|symmetric monoidal]].<ref name=montgomery1993/><ref>{{cite arXiv |last1=Andruskiewitsch |first1=Nicolas |title=Triangular Hopf algebras with the Chevalley property |date=2002-07-12 |last2=Etingof |first2=Pavel |last3=Gelaki |first3=Shlomo |eprint=math/0008232 }}</ref>
These facts can be taken as motivation for studying Hopf algebras.

== Definition and basic properties ==
A representation of a Hopf algebra <math>H</math> over a field <math>K</math> is a <math>K</math>-[[vector space]] <math>V</math> with an [[Semigroup action|action]] <math>H \times V \to V</math> usually denoted by juxtaposition (that is, the image of <math>(h,v)</math> is written <math>hv</math>) that is compatible with the vector space structures of <math>H</math> and <math>V</math>. The vector space <math>V</math> is called an <math>H</math>-module.

The module structure of a representation of a Hopf algebra <math>H</math> is simply its structure as a module for the underlying associative algebra. The main use of considering the additional structure of a Hopf algebra is when considering all <math>H</math>-modules as a category. The additional structure is also used to define invariant elements of an <math>H</math>-module <math>V</math>. An element <math>v</math> in <math>V</math> is [[Invariant (mathematics)|invariant]] under <math>H</math> if for all <math>h</math> in <math>H</math>, <math>hv = \epsilon(h)v</math>, where <math>\epsilon</math> is the [[counit]] of <math>H</math>. The subset of all invariant elements of <math>V</math> forms a submodule of <math>V</math>.

== Relation to the representation theory of other structures ==

Hopf algebra representations are a generalisation of both [[Representation theory of finite groups|representations of finite groups]] and those of [[Lie algebra representation|Lie algebras]]. For a fixed underlying [[Field (mathematics)|field]] <math>K</math>, the representations of a finite group <math>G</math> are in one-to-one correspondence with those of its [[Group ring#Group algebra over a finite group|group algebra]] <math>KG</math>. Similarly, the representations of a Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> are in one-to-one correspondence with those of its [[universal enveloping algebra]] <math>U(\mathfrak{g})</math>. 
Both <math>KG</math> and <math>U(\mathfrak{g})</math> are in turn Hopf algebras, and many types of Hopf algebra, such as [[quantum groups]], arise as deformations or "quantisations" of these classical examples.

Like [[Group representations|representations of groups]], Lie algebras and [[quantum group]]s, one can take [[Dual representation|duals]] and [[Tensor product of representations|tensor products]] of representations of a Hopf algebra, and there exist trivial representations which act as multiplicative units with respect to the tensor product. These operations do not exist for the representations of more general associative algebras.

== Categories of representations as a motivation for Hopf algebras ==
For an associative algebra <math>H</math>, the [[tensor product]] <math>V_1\otimes V_2</math> of two <math>H </math>-modules <math>V_1</math> and <math>V_2</math> is a vector space, but not necessarily an <math>H</math>-module. For the tensor product to be a [[functor]]ial product operation on <math>H</math>-modules, there must be a linear binary operation <math>\Delta:H\to H\otimes H</math> such that for any <math>v_i</math> in <math>V_i</math> and any <math>h\in H</math>,
: <math>hv=\Delta(h)(v_1\otimes v_2)=h_{(1)}v_1\otimes h_{(2)}v_2,</math>
and for any <math>v_i\in V_i</math> and <math>a,b\in H</math>
: <math>\Delta(ab)(v_1\otimes v_2)=(ab)v=a(b(v))=\Delta(a)(\Delta(b)(v_1\otimes v_2))=(\Delta(a)\Delta(b))(v_1\otimes v_2).</math>
using sumless [[Sweedler's notation]], which is somewhat like an index free form of the [[Einstein summation convention]]. This is satisfied if there is a <math>\Delta</math> such that <math>\Delta(ab)=\Delta(a)\Delta(b)</math> for all <math>a,b\in H</math>.

For the category of <math>H</math>-modules to be a [[monoidal category]] with respect to <math>\otimes</math>, there must be natural isomorphisms (called associators) between <math>V_1\otimes(V_2\otimes V_3)</math> and <math>(V_1\otimes V_2)\otimes V_3</math> for all <math>V_i</math>, and there must be unit object <math>\epsilon_H</math>, called the trivial module, such that for any module <math>V</math> there are natural isomorphisms between <math>\epsilon_H\otimes V</math>, <math>V</math> and <math>V\otimes\epsilon_H</math>. 

This means that for <math>v_1\otimes v_2\otimes v_3</math> in
: <math>V_1\otimes(V_2\otimes V_3)=(V_1\otimes V_2)\otimes V_3,</math>
(where we use the natural identification of vector spaces) and for <math>h</math> in <math>H</math>,
: <math>((\operatorname{id}\otimes \Delta)\Delta(h))(v_1\otimes v_2\otimes v_3)
= ((\Delta\otimes \operatorname{id}) \Delta(h)) (v_1\otimes v_2\otimes v_3),</math>
or in Sweedler notation,
: <math>h_{(1)}v_1\otimes h_{(2)(1)}v_2\otimes h_{(2)(2)}v_3
= h_{(1)(1)}v_1\otimes h_{(1)(2)}v_2\otimes h_{(2)}v_3.</math>

This will hold for any three <math>H</math>-modules if <math>\Delta</math> satisfies 
: <math>(\operatorname{id}\otimes \Delta)\Delta = (\Delta \otimes \operatorname{id})\Delta.</math>

The trivial module must be one-dimensional, and so an [[algebra homomorphism]] <math>\epsilon:H\to K</math> may be defined such that <math>hv=\epsilon(h)v</math> for all <math>v\in\epsilon_H</math>. The trivial module may be identified with <math>K</math>, with <math>1</math> being the element such that <math>1\otimes v = v = v\otimes 1</math> for all <math>v</math>. For the desired property, we require that for any <math>v</math> in any <math>H</math>-module <math>V</math>, any <math>c\in\epsilon_H</math> and any <math>h\in H</math>,
: <math>(\varepsilon(h_{(1)})h_{(2)})cv = h_{(1)}c\otimes h_{(2)}v = h(c\otimes v) = h(cv),</math>
and similarly
: <math>(h_{(1)}\varepsilon(h_{(2)}))cv = h(cv).</math>

The existence of an algebra homomorphism <math>\epsilon</math> satisfying 
: <math>\varepsilon(h_{(1)})h_{(2)} = h = h_{(1)}\varepsilon(h_{(2)})</math> 
is a sufficient condition for the existence of the trivial module. 

It follows that in order for the category of <math>H</math>-modules to be a monoidal category with respect to the tensor product, it is sufficient for <math>H</math> to have maps <math>\Delta</math> and <math>\epsilon</math> satisfying these conditions. This is the motivation for the definition of a [[bialgebra]], where <math>\Delta</math> is called the [[comultiplication]] and <math>\epsilon</math> is called the [[counit]].

In order for each <math>H</math>-module <math>V</math> to have a [[dual representation]] <math>V</math> such that the underlying vector spaces are dual and the operation * is functorial over the monoidal category of <math>H</math>-modules, there must be a linear map <math>S:H\to H</math> such that for any <math>h\in H</math>, <math>x\in V</math> and <math>y\in V^*</math>,
: <math>\langle y, S(h)x\rangle = \langle hy, x \rangle.</math>
where <math>\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle</math> is the usual [[pairing]] of dual vector spaces. If the map <math>\varphi:V\otimes V^*\rightarrow \varepsilon_H</math> induced by the pairing is to be an <math>H</math>-homomorphism, then for any <math>h\in H</math>, <math>x\in V</math> and <math>y\in V^*</math>,
: <math>\varphi\left(h(x\otimes y)\right)=\varphi\left(x\otimes S(h_{(1)})h_{(2)}y\right)=\varphi\left(S(h_{(2)})h_{(1)}x\otimes y\right)=h\varphi(x\otimes y)=\varepsilon(h)\varphi(x\otimes y),</math>
which is satisfied if 
: <math>S(h_{(1)})h_{(2)}=\varepsilon(h)=h_{(1)}S(h_{(2)})</math> 
for all <math>h\in H</math>.

If there is such a map <math>S</math>, then it is called an ''antipode'', and <math>H</math> is a Hopf algebra. The desire for a monoidal category of modules with functorial tensor products and dual representations is therefore one motivation for the concept of a Hopf algebra.

== Representations on an algebra ==
A Hopf algebra also has representations which carry additional structure, namely they are algebras.

Let <math>H</math> be a Hopf algebra over a field <math>K</math>, let <math>A</math> be a (unital) associative [[algebra over a field|algebra]] over <math>K</math> with the product operation <math>\mu: A\otimes A  \to A</math> (and unit map <math>u:K\to A</math>), and suppose that <math>\rho: H\otimes A \to A</math> is a representation of <math>H</math> on <math>A</math>. From the discussion above, <math>A\otimes A</math> is naturally an <math>H</math>-module. We say that <math>\rho</math> is a '''representation of <math>H</math> on an algebra''', or that <math>A</math> is an '''<math>H</math>-module algebra''', if <math>\mu</math> is <math>H</math>-[[equivariant]] (and <math>u</math> is also equivariant, or equivalently <math>\rho(h,1_A) = \epsilon(h) 1_A</math>).<ref name=montgomery1993/> As special cases, Lie algebras, Lie superalgebras and groups can also have representations on an algebra.

== Comodules and Hopf modules ==
Dual to the notion of a representation or module of an algebra is that of a '''coreprepresentation''' or '''[[comodule]]''' of a coalgebra. Since Hopf algebras are bialgebras, they can have both modules and comodules, and as for modules, trivial comodules and tensor products and dual of comodules exist. If <math>H</math> is a finite-dimensional Hopf algebra, its dual <math>H^*</math> is also a Hopf algebra; <math>H</math>-modules are then <math>H^*</math>-modules and vice-versa. A weaker version of this statement holds for the infinite-dimensional case, where <math>H^*</math> must be replaced with a smaller space <math>H^\circ</math> called the finite dual.<ref name=montgomery1993/>

A '''Hopf module''' for a Hopf algebra <math>H</math> is a vector space which is both an <math>H</math>-module and an <math>H</math>-comodule satisfying the compatibility condition that the comodule map <math>\rho: M \to H\otimes M</math> is <math>H</math>-equivariant. A fundamental result says that Hopf modules are [[Free module|free]] as ordinary modules; the utility of this fact is that it can be used to prove that a particular <math>H</math>-module is free.<ref name=montgomery1993/>
